Cool idea! I approve of the privacy oriented design. But it looks like you didn’t actually test this on iOS as automatic text correction is completely broken.

mbreese · Nov 7, 2026

There’s no better way to get a lot of testers than to have a Show HN.

I’ll confirm - there are cursor bugs on iOS. Both on newlines and autocorrect.

I’m personally more forgiving of an LLM “helped” site, if it looks like there was a human in the loop for the process. An LLM has more context about the design goals and architecture than the reader, so if it’s an informative page, I’m not personally bothered.

But I’m probably in the minority.

pcj-github · Nov 7, 2026

I wrote a similar tool to this many years ago that used JATS as an internal document model, using contentEditable, and I can relate to the pain you refer to. Getting the semantics right in cases where you split or join text that has varying types of nested context was hard.

I like what you did here in terms of the cursor that points one way or the other: it tells you if you're in "normal" mode, or for example, in a bold region. I don't think I've seen that before so, if you made it up, that itself is a cool invention.

hnlmorg · Nov 7, 2026

This looks slick but I think you need a better way to market it.

The 2D canvas part is the norm for anyone who wants performance. Working with the DOM becomes painfully slow and resource intensive the moment you add syntax highlighting, spell checking, and other visual chrome, to large documents.

This is why Monaco (the editor widget behind VSCode) is a canvas. Why terminal emulators built with web technologies use canvas. And so on.

So I wouldn’t say the canvas part of the heading is a differentiator.

chrismorgan · Nov 7, 2026

> The 2D canvas part is the norm for anyone who wants performance. Working with the DOM becomes painfully slow and resource intensive the moment you add syntax highlighting, spell checking, and other visual chrome, to large documents.

This is wildly wrong. 2D canvas is consistently slower than letting the browser handle the rendering, so long as you avoid making the DOM too complex, and possibly monitor the viewport and only keep some of the content in the DOM at a time (though for most applications it’s somewhere between harmful and not useful, and it definitely adds a lot of complexity).

> This is why Monaco (the editor widget behind VSCode) is a canvas.

It isn’t.

> Why terminal emulators built with web technologies use canvas.

Why on earth would you build with web technology, if you’re then going to use canvas? I can’t immediately think of any that match your description (though I have no doubt that in-browser ones using canvas exist).

gb2d_hn · Nov 7, 2026

This looks great. I've been impressed at how flexible CodeMirror is though. When I started EtherPK (https://app.etherpk.com) I made a bet that CodeMirror could help me build an editor that could combine outliner blocks, standard prose and rich overlays / graphics / embeds in one editor. I was concerned that I'd hit a road block (I presumed Logseq used custom HTML, nested divs and click position mapping for rendered text to the underlying input for a reason), but 9 months in I couldn't be happier with my choice, and it's a blazing fast editor that feels really nice and light to type in (live demo: https://app.etherpk.com/demo)
